notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Numbers 1:1–27, but there are gaps you should know about first.

- **Missing sources:** I couldn't read anything on this passage from the Catholic or Orthodox sites, the NET Bible notes, the Lutheran or Pentecostal sites, or about prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those are left out. I also couldn't read the main page of NET Bible notes, so it's not quoted directly.
- **No real Protestant disagreement found:** The Baptist (Gill), Methodist (Wesley) and Calvary Chapel (Guzik) sources I read agree on what these verses mean. The one big debate, how to read the large numbers, divides commentators across all traditions rather than along church lines.

**v. 1**
- **The date.** The tabernacle went up on the first day of the first month (Exodus 40:17). This order came one month later, so all the laws in Leviticus must have been given within that one month. This is Adam Clarke, quoted by Guzik. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/
- **Timing in more detail.** The Pulpit Commentary puts it on the first day of Zif (or Ijar). That is a year and two weeks after the exodus, ten and a half months after arriving at Sinai, and a month after the tabernacle went up. https://biblehub.com/numbers/1-1.htm
- **The tent's name.** Ellicott says it is called the "tent of meeting" because it was where God met with Moses. https://biblehub.com/numbers/1-1.htm
- **The book's theme.** Guzik notes the Hebrew title of the book is "In the Wilderness." The wilderness was a place to pass through, not to settle in. He also notes that the phrase "the LORD spoke to Moses" appears more than 150 times in Numbers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/
- **A royal picture.** Matthew Henry pictures God giving the order from "his royal palace," the tabernacle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/1-1.html

**v. 2**
- **Not the same count as Exodus 38.** Wesley says this is a different count from the one in Exodus 38:26. That one happened before the tabernacle was built; this one happened after. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/numbers-1.html
- **The earlier count.** The Pulpit Commentary says an earlier half-shekel tax on adult men had already anticipated this count. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/1-2.html
- **Counting by families.** Guzik says the count was made by families because Israel's strength depended on the strength of each family. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/
- **Why God ordered it here but punished David's census.** A sermon quoted on Bible Hub (Lewis R. Dunn) says God ordered this census himself. David's later census was prompted by Satan and done out of personal pride. https://biblehub.com/sermons/numbers/1-2.htm
- **Two purposes.** That sermon page also says the count showed how fully God kept his promise to multiply Abraham's descendants. It also separated true Israelites from the "mixed multitude" travelling with them. https://biblehub.com/sermons/numbers/1-2.htm

**v. 3**
- **Age limits.** Gill reads the verse as twenty and older with no upper limit. He notes that some limited it to fifty or sixty. Aben Ezra adds that the words "in Israel" leave out the mixed multitude. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-3.htm
- **Under-twenties and the unfit.** Matthew Henry says God spared those under twenty out of kindness to their youth. The old, sick and disabled were not counted either. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/1-13.html
- **Every citizen a soldier.** The Pulpit Commentary says, "Every citizen was a soldier." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-3.htm
- **An army of the Lord.** Keil & Delitzsch say the tribes were being organised as the Lord's hosts, so the whole people could fight for him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-3.htm
- **Not victory by numbers.** Guzik says Israel would win the land by God's hand, not by superior forces, but they still had to fight. He applies this to taking an honest stock of one's spiritual strength. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/
- **The key phrase.** Precept Austin says "go out to war" is the key phrase of the chapter, used 14 times. It adds that this generation would later die in the wilderness because of unbelief. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-1-commentary
- **Spiritual reading.** Gill and Henry both read the counted men as a picture of the church as an army ("church militant"). This is a difference of emphasis, not a dispute. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/1-13.html

**v. 4**
- **A kind of representative government.** Guzik says each tribal head was in effect the tribe's chieftain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/
- **Different from the earlier count.** Barnes (on Bible Hub) says this count was overseen by one assessor from each tribe, not by the Levites. It was meant to serve civil and military purposes, not only religious ones. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-3.htm

**vv. 5–15**
- **Twelve tribes without Levi.** Levi is missing, but there are still twelve because Joseph's line splits into Ephraim and Manasseh. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/
- **The leaders' names.** Guzik says almost all the names refer to God and show a believing community. Examples: Elizur, "My God is a Rock"; Shelumiel, "My Peace is God"; Nethanel, "Gift of God." He quotes Trapp: these men had not forgotten God's name even in slavery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/

**v. 7**
- **Nahshon.** The Pulpit Commentary says he was Aaron's brother-in-law (Exodus 6:23) and an ancestor of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/1.htm

**v. 10**
- **Elishama.** Guzik says he was Joshua's grandfather (1 Chronicles 7:26–27). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/

**v. 16**
- **Chosen by their tribes?** Guzik thinks it likely the tribe heads were elected by their tribes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/
- **"Thousands" or "divisions"?** In this verse the KJV has "heads of thousands," while the NASB has "heads of divisions." It is the same Hebrew word (*eleph*) at the centre of the debate over the numbers in v. 21. https://biblehub.com/hebrew/505.htm

**vv. 17–18**
- **Done in one day.** The Pulpit Commentary says the natural reading is that the count was finished in one day. That means the family lists were ready beforehand, made up when the tax was paid. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/numbers-1.html
- **Recording ancestry.** Keil & Delitzsch say "recorded their ancestry" means having oneself entered in the family records. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-20.htm
- **Each person counted.** Guzik stresses "one by one": every individual mattered to God, not just the final total. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/

**v. 19**
- **Obedience.** The Pulpit Commentary says "as the LORD commanded" marks the basic difference between this count and David's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/1.htm
- **Motives matter.** Bible Hub's own notes say David's later census shows that motives matter, while Israel's first count was done in dependence on God. https://biblehub.com/numbers/1-45.htm

**v. 20**
- **Order of the list.** Gill says the tribes were counted in the order they would camp. Simeon and Gad follow Reuben because they camped under Reuben's banner. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-20.htm
- **Reuben's place.** Gill notes that Reuben, though firstborn, had fewer men than six other tribes, which fits Jacob's words in Genesis 49:4. Bullinger agrees that Reuben lost his rank and is "not many in number here." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-20.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bul/numbers-1.html
- **Reformed reading.** A Ligonier devotional, citing Calvin, says Reuben's sin cost him first place, but God kept him as one of the twelve tribes (Num 1:20–21). https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/one-sin-twelve-sons
- **"Generations."** Ellicott says the word means all the descendants of the tribe's founder. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-20.htm

**v. 21: the big question of the numbers**
- **The traditional view.**
  - Guzik estimates the whole people at 2–2.5 million. He lists the main views: the numbers are literal; they come from David's or Solomon's time; they are code (gematria), exaggeration or symbol; or the word *eleph* means something other than "thousand." He also lists copying errors, but says no surviving manuscript supports that. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-1/
  - Bible Hub's Q&A says Jews and Christians have mainly read *eleph* as "thousand" and defends the numbers as literal. https://biblehub.com/q/do_numbers_1_figures_match_smaller_counts.htm
  - Constable says there is no obvious solution, but chooses to read "thousands" unless better evidence turns up. https://studylight.org/commentaries/dcc/numbers-1.html
- **Rounded figures.** Constable thinks Moses rounded the numbers. Matthew Henry suggests counting by the rulers of hundreds and fifties (Exodus 18:25) produced round numbers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/1-27.html
- **The smaller-number view.** GotQuestions explains this view. If *eleph* means "clan," Reuben would have 500 fighting men from 46 family groups. That would make the whole people about 30,000. The problems: it requires a copying error in v. 46, and some say the Hebrew grammar demands "thousand." https://www.gotquestions.org/Israelites-exodus.html
- **Modern scholarship.**
  - Bible Odyssey says counting people in the Hebrew Bible was seen as both sacred and dangerous. That may explain why the Levites are not counted (1:49) and why Exodus 30:12 requires a ransom payment to prevent a plague. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/counting-and-censuses-in-the-hebrew-bible/
  - Hastings' Dictionary, an older critical source, credits these chapters to a "Priestly" writer and calls the figures "artificial and impossible." https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdb/n/numbers-book-of.html

**vv. 22–23**
- **Shorter wording.** Gill notes that Simeon's entry drops the words "by their polls, every male." After two mentions the reader is meant to assume them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-20.htm
- **A tribe that shrank.** Simeon's 59,300 later fell to 22,200 in the second census (Numbers 26). Chuck Smith notes it was "more than halved." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/1-6.html

**vv. 24–25**
- **Gad's odd figure.** Gad's total is the only one not rounded to the hundred; it ends in fifty, for reasons no one knows (Guzik). https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/numbers/numbers-1.cfm
- **Barnes's explanation.** Barnes puts the uneven figure down to Gad's herding, wandering way of life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/1-27.html
- **Gad's place in the list.** Hastings says Gad is listed here, not with its usual partners, because chapter 2 camps it next to Reuben and Simeon. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdb/n/numbers-book-of.html

**vv. 26–27**
- **Judah the largest tribe.** Wesley (Methodist) says Judah was "far more than any other tribe," fulfilling Jacob's prophecy in Genesis 49:8–12. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/1-27.html
- **Gill agrees.** Gill (Baptist) links Judah's growth to the coming ruler and the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/1-20.htm
- **Henry's comparison.** Matthew Henry notes Judah had more than double Benjamin's and Manasseh's numbers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/1-27.html
- **Why Judah matters.** GotQuestions says Judah stayed faithful longer than the other tribes and was the tribe Jesus came from. https://www.gotquestions.org/Numbers-census.html
- **A sermon note.** The Bible Hub sermon page adds that only Caleb and Joshua, out of this huge army, survived the coming years of unbelief. https://biblehub.com/sermons/numbers/1-2.htm
